content:
In some parts of the United States, it still feels like 1920. When the federal government repealed Prohibition in 1933, it left the decision on how to legislate the production and sale of wine, beer, and spirits to the individual states. State governments then handed alcohol regulation to towns, counties, and other municipalities, and laws on drinking diversified to a fine-tooth comb level across the country. A “dry” county, meaning it prohibits the sale of alcoholic beverages, could neighbor a fully “wet” county, one that permits the sale of alcoholic beverages.

Ninety-three years later, some counties across the U.S. are still dry, and the reasons behind the abstinences range from historic to religious.

Below, we mapped out the 47 counties in the U.S. that still prohibit the sale of alcohol. What is most evident at first glance is the concentration of teetotalling neighborhoods in the South, along what’s otherwise known as the “Bible Belt,” dubbed so because of the region’s high density of practicing Christians. In Arkansas, the state with the most dry counties at 29, sects like Methodists, Baptists, and Evangelicals — the latter makes up roughly 50 percent of Arkansas’ population — have promoted abstaining from alcohol since the 1800s. In 1831, local churches in the state aligned to form the Little Rock Temperance Society.

Temperance was also historically associated with the women’s rights movement of the mid-19th century, particularly in Kentucky, where there are six dry counties. Advocates of a prohibition warned of how alcohol worsened some men’s maltreatment of women at home. One Kentucky native, Carrie Nation, famously wielded a hatchet around towns, hacking at the walls and doors at saloons and clubs.

Some counties returned to teetotalism after Prohibition’s repeal. In Arkansas’ Craighead and Crawford counties, current accounts attribute the alcohol ban to municipal votes that occurred in 1944 when many American men were overseas fighting in the Second World War, and at-combat soldiers could not cast their ballots. Since then, petitions to turn wet have yet to amass enough voters. Just getting the question to permit alcohol on ballots in certain counties requires a much larger percentage of voters than most other issues.

Other reasons that some counties across the U.S. remain dry include low population and lobbying from successful liquor stores in nearby wet counties who fear losing business, among others.

The map below omits the in-between examples, referred to as “moist” counties. While these counties are de jure dry, they leave the decision up to each local government, so regulations vary from town to town. The map does include dry counties that allow special permits to certain on-premise accounts, such as country clubs, restaurants, and other businesses.

This is VinePair’s Booze News Weekly Roundup, where we gather the hottest headlines and product releases every Friday for a snapshot of what’s happening in the beverage alcohol industry. This week, we have updates on Diageo slashing its workforce by six percent, Samuel Adams workers’ intent to unionize, the latest product releases, and more.

News to know:

  • Americans’ drinking rate remains at rock bottom: A Gallup poll found 54 percent of drinking-age Americans consume alcohol, the same rate as last year’s record low since 1939. The analytics and advisory firm included a question on nonalcoholic beverage consumption for the first time in its annual survey and found only 17 percent of U.S. citizens substituted a zero-proof wine, beer, or spirit for an alcoholic drink at least once in the past year.
  • Diageo cuts roughly 2,000 jobs in restructuring plan: The global spirits giant slimmed its workforce by six percent year-over-year through the end of June, according to its annual report. The results come after Diageo chief executive officer Dave Lewis denied to disclose the number of roles the overhaul would affect when announcing a $1 billion savings plan involving reducing prices and cutting jobs. According to Reuters, the company is set to complete its workforce reduction by Sept. 1, meaning it’s possible the number of impacted jobs can increase.
  • Boston Beer Company workers plan to unionize: Employees at the Samuel Adams Boston Brewery in Jamaica Plain, Mass. — Boston Beer Co.’s first and flagship brewery — filed an intent to unionize to the parent company last Thursday. Workers included in the possible union include bartenders, cooks, beer ambassadors, and key holders, according to the United Food and Commercial Workers Union Local 328, who first reported on the filing. The organization would be the second Samuel Adams location with a union.
  • Sazerac to ink a deal with Welsh vodka brand: The Louisville, Ky.-based spirits company agreed to acquire Au Vodka, a buzzy brand in the U.K., for a reported £500 million ($681 million). Au Vodka will join Sazerac’s portfolio well-stocked in brands geared toward Gen Z drinkers like BuzzBallz and sipMARGS.

Product releases to watch:

  • Pernod Ricard ships Single Pot Still Jameson to U.S. shores: Jameson, the leading Irish whiskey brand by volume, is debuting its Distiller’s Batch bottling in American markets. Distiller’s Batch is part of the brand’s premium Reserve Series and will be available nationwide in September.
  • Sazerac forays into soju: The American spirits conglomerate is entering the soju category with the launch of DAHLO, as demand for the Korean liquor is on the rise. DAHLO’s inaugural flavors are original, peach, strawberry, and lychee, and each 375-milliliter bottle retails for around $5.99.

content:
Made with a commitment to both honoring tradition and embracing innovation, G4 Tequila is the latest brand to win over the bar industry amid the artisanal tequila renaissance.

With deep family roots in the industry, Felipe Camarena founded the distillery that houses G4’s production in 2007 before its official opening in 2011. The brand didn’t reach shelves in the United States until 2014, but in the past decade, it’s become one of the foremost choices among bar pros and tequila enthusiasts.

G4 aims to honor the history and tradition of tequila while ushering the spirit into the new age, converging old-school ingredients and techniques with new-school technology. From the meaning behind the name to the brand’s meticulous production methods, here are seven things to know about G4 Tequila.

  1. The name refers to Camarena’s family lineage.

    Felipe Camarena is the great-grandson of Don Pedro Camarena, a legendary tequilero often credited with being among the first to bring Blue Weber agave to the highlands in the 19th century. The family has continued in the business over the years, making Felipe Camarena the fourth generation to work in the tequila industry, inspiring the name “G4.”

    Don Pedro built the Camarena family’s first distillery in Los Altos, before it crumbled upon the onset of the Mexican Revolution in 1910. Don Pedro’s son, also named Felipe, opened the family’s second distillery, La Alteña, which is now home to brands like Tapatio and Tequila Ocho. Felipe used to work at La Alteña, but left in 2007 to construct his own distillery, El Pandillo.

  2. You’ll be drinking rainwater — sort of.

    G4 — and all brands produced at El Pandillo, for that matter — sources both spring water and rainwater to make its tequila. The brand’s blanco expression uses a half-and-half split between the two water types, which its website says helps create “an authentic, beyond-organic experience.” Other accounts agree and call it the “secret” to its greatness, saying the rainwater imparts a “wet-stone minerality” to the spirit. El Pandillo retrieves rainwater through a capturing system built on the distillery’s roof, funneling it into a 200,000-liter underground tank.

  3. The master distiller invented a custom agave-crushing machine.

    Camarena studied engineering and used his gadget-building side to invent an agave crusher. Named Felipestein as a nod to “Frankenstein,” the machine is 19,000-pounds, built entirely from recycled parts of a railroad car, steamroller, and other industrial materials. Felipestein, studded with spikes, rolls along rail tracks, crushing cooked agave along the way. Camarena has found that this unique method presses the plant’s juices without tearing its fibers.

  4. G4 uses an ancestral yeast strain.

    Camarena dials into his family’s tequila-making legacy even further by using a strain of agave yeast preserved from his grandfather, Don Felipe, who opened La Alteña in 1937. Don Felipe passed down the yeast for generations, helping preserve the Camarena family’s identity in its tequilas.

  5. The brand has a proprietary tequila certification course.

    G4 collaborated with the International Tequila Academy to form its own training curriculum for tequila-interested consumers. Retailers, bartenders, or aficionados who simply want to learn more about the brand, its history, and process, can follow the online course. The curriculum covers tequila production, G4’s products, and the ins and outs of the spirits market.

  6. G4’s site features the one surviving piece of the Camarena family’s original distillery.

    Little remains of Don Pedro Camarena’s original distillery that burned down during the Mexican Revolution. One of its remnants is the volcanic stone tahona that was used at the Los Altos location — it was the tool the family used to make its first-ever batch of tequila. The tahona is now on display at El Pandillo.

  7. The brand is expanding — and adding new products.

    Given its smashing popularity in recent years, G4 is scaling upward, and along with this growth came a new storage facility that neighbors El Pandillo. There, G4 is experimenting with different aging techniques and barrel types. For example, it recently announced that it will mature some of its tequila in lightly used Jack Daniel’s casks. It will also experiment with other vessels, including ex-Cognac, sherry, and wine barrels.

content:
For years, the comedian Ron White has done a joke about the time he almost got in a plane crash. It’s an all-timer that unravels over the course of a few minutes, and you really owe it to yourself to watch the whole thing. I hate to spoil the punch line, but the joke is about 30 years old, so with respect to Mr. White, here goes:

The guy sitting next to me is losing his mind. Apparently, he had a lot to live for.

He goes, “Hey man … huh-huh-huh … hey man … huh-huh-huh … If one of these engines fails, how far will the other one take us?”

[I said] “All the way to the scene of the crash … which is pretty handy, because that’s where we’re headed. I bet we beat the paramedics there by a half hour.”

Classic stuff. And unfortunately clarifying stuff for the situation at Tilray Brands, whose overstuffed portfolio of craft breweries is well on its way to where it was always headed.

Last week, news broke that the Canadian vice conglomerate planned to close Terrapin Beer Company’s 100,000-square-foot production facility in Athens, Ga. The University of Georgia’s independent student-run paper, The Red & Black, first clocked the shutdown notice, which was buried in Tilray’s most recent 10-K filing. The document also flagged previous consolidations and closures at Hop Valley, Revolver, and Redhook, as well as Atwater, which wasn’t “closed” so much as “hastily sold back to its owners less than two years after it was acquired.” But forget the semantics, let’s talk strategy, because it’s pretty complicated. Just kidding: we’re cutting costs, kids!

Shortly after cobbling together its island of misfit breweries from the wreckage of macrobrewers’ salad-days craft beer ambitions, Tilray embarked upon Project 420, which is not the Heritage Foundation’s plan to make smoking weed a capital offense but rather a goofily named corporate savings strategy. (SweetWater Brewing, its first major acquisition in the segment in 2020, does a 420 Extra Pale Ale and a 420 Fest, too. You get it.) Midway through 2025, the firm’s garrulous chief executive, Irwin Simon, told investors that he was targeting some $33 million in cuts, which doesn’t sound like a lot until you remember it’s almost half of what he paid for an eight-brand gaggle of Anheuser-Busch InBev also-rans just a couple years prior. By the end of February 2026, the company’s filing reads, “we considered the Project 420 plan to be completed due to reaching the cost savings target that we had set out to achieve even though there are still ongoing initiatives relating to additional cost savings, SKU rationalization and distributor rationalization.” Whether Terrapin’s closure is technically part of Project 420, or whatever its new-and-reduced successor program is called within the halls of Tilray headquarters is irrelevant for our purposes. It’s another cut.

Pour one out for Terrapin’s poor workers and fans, who have been through the wringer over the past decade as the company went from a Southeastern craft-brewing darling to an odious sellout to big bad Molson Coors, to a cast-off has-been when Simon and company came calling in the summer of 2024. But where there’s sorrow, there should be little surprise. Simon’s “regional jewel” thesis for batting cleanup on the craft-brewing industry’s second boom, which he articulated to Hop Take in December 2024, never made sense without major cuts, even at the bargain-basement purchase prices he was able to command from the bigs as they bolted for flavored malt beverages and spirits-based canned cocktails. This wasn’t something Tilray was openly talking about at that point, mind you, but it was evident even then. As I wrote:

Whatever Tilray does to burnish its “regional jewels” in bars, restaurants, and sports venues will ultimately have to be judged by whether it successfully repositions those brands for distributed sales — and whether it can actually drive down its costs like Simon claims.

The latter is absurd on face: Tilray lacks the buying power of ABI or MC (or Constellation, Heineken, Pabst… ), and its operations are scattered across many small locations rather than a few big ones. Simon concedes that point to Hop Take, but insists that Tilray can unlock savings anyway by integrating these brands into a national operation in a way their former corporate masters failed to.

More than a year and a half later, whatever sweet synergies Tilray has been able to capture with its mid-major scale have paled in comparison to those savings it has been able to extract from the business in the form of layoffs, plant closures, and portfolio weed-outs. This hasn’t come cheaply, mind you. As my VinePair colleague Stephen Bradley noted, “Tilray disclosed it spent $6.8 million in Project 420 restructuring costs in fiscal year 2026, which ended May 31.” That’s on top of the $8.5 million it already spent on the slash-a-rama in 2025, per the 10-K.

This spend-and-shed pattern has become a bit of a calling card for Tilray, which earlier this year acquired BrewDog at the rock-bottom price of~ $54 million and announced a deal to brew Carlsberg stateside shortly thereafter. Even as it was culling its craft-brewing herd, in other words, it was adding to it. The results have been mixed. The company’s beverage business grew net revenue by six percent year-over-year for its 2026 fiscal year, which ran through May; its gross profit was down two percent for the same period. But that’s including the big ol’ boost that BrewDog delivered to its stat-sheet. (Here too, another calling card of Simon and company: before the dust can really settle on the previous fiscal year’s acquisitions, he’s already bought something else, juicing the topline numbers while making it harder to benchmark the firm against its actual performance in the marketplace.) The drinks business remains “one of Tilray’s most important growth engines,” Simon told investors on an earnings call late last month, and is “still in the early stages of unlocking the full potential of this business.”

That may sound good to Wall Street. (Or not: Tilray’s troubled stock declined a smidge following the July 28 call, before rallying more recently.) But it rings ominous when you consider how the company has made it this far on its craft-brewing side-quest. While it waits and hopes for federal legalization of recreational cannabis, it has to make its mismatched semi-national network of breweries produce meaningful revenue. It can only book the savings from closing each brewery once. At some point, Tilray must squeeze actual, consistent profit out of these brands. I thought — and still do — that the company had lined up plenty of runway by buying into the segment at such firesale prices. It has lined up more still with all its cuts. But whether anybody wants what’s left on the other side of the butcher counter remains to be seen. The sales data suggest, ah, maybe not. Year-to-date through July 12, Tilray’s portfolio is down 13.7 percent in dollars and 14.8 percent by volume in multi-outlet grocery, mass retail, and convenience stores tracked by the market research firm Circana. Those declines dramatically overshadow the overall beer category and the craft-brewing segment

This is the rub. “With robust brewing operations across the country, this transition allows us to continue serving customers efficiently while leveraging the scale and capabilities of our broader brewery footprint,” chief corporate affairs officer Berrin Noorata told Brewbound in a statement. The optimization jargon tracks with the basics of the brewing business: it is a scale business. But while sending Terrapin’s brewhouse to the Hopsecutioner may carve out costs, it also hollows out the brand itself. Even with healthy brands — which Tilray’s, by and large, are not — it’s hard to tell muscle from fat. But in a down market this competitive, shuttering a hometown brewery promises some real rough turbulence.

This was always where Tilray was headed. Where it goes next remains to be seen.

🤯 Hop-ocalypse Now

Summer 2026 has not been kind to Bud Light, what with its bleak bloodsport-’n-bigotry sponsorship of the Trump administration’s Ultimate Fighting Championship circus on the White House lawn, and of course the brand’s ongoing declines as both the American drinking public and parent company Anheuser-Busch InBev shift their focus to stuff like Michelob Ultra, Cutwater, and BeatBox. Complicating matters further, one of the celebrities the brand hired to chud up its image in the wake of 2023’s right-wing transphobia tantrum, comedian Shane Gillis, last week spoke out against Truth Social’s transparently corrupt scheme to sell early access to Trump’s posts on the platform, calling it “literally insider trading.” And on an episode of “The Joe Rogan Experience,” no less! Awkward stuff for a brand that has been desperately cozying up to the MAGA-verse for the past three years.

📈 Ups…

TailGate Brewery is telling a Tennessee success story, up 40 percent in distribution year-over-year through the first half of 2026… Garage Beer released an apple-flavored version, because who doesn’t want free money?… Hi-Wire Brewing is taking over production and sales for Appalachian Mountain Brewery as craft consolidation continues…

📉 …and downs

Boston Beer Company’s chief financial officer is headed for the exit… Ardagh Metal Packaging is on the auction block…

Drinking beers and household chores never had much in common, but now, you can “set the table” while knocking back a half-goblet of lager. In the latest beer challenge to sweep the internet, people are guzzling Birra Moretti in an attempt to align the liquid’s surface with the mustachioed man on the beer’s label. The goal: make it look like his arm is resting on a table of beer.

This trend offers a new spin on Guinness’ megawatt “splitting the G” phenomenon, roughly two years after the now-iconic gulping-guessing game swarmed pubs and social media platforms. The challenge likely emerged as a bar game, but it appears to have become a worldwide fad after popular TikTok and Instagram accounts posted carousels and videos of successful table-sets and garnered tens of thousands of views and likes.

@the.white.horse.southill Drink responsibly kings and queens ✌🏻 #fyp #moretti #beer #hospitality #pub ♬ original sound – Ibiza Records

Just as some devotees met “splitting the G” with disdain, certain beer purists are gawking at the challenge. “Can’t you just drink your beer like a normal person?,” one Instagram user commented on LADBible’s post, the first to broadcast the challenge.

While you can find a solid pint of Guinness in a branded glass to partake in “splitting the G” at just about any pub, hunting down Birra Moretti in the signature goblet isn’t as easy. But with “setting the table” on the rise, the brand is only poised to become more popular.

The Heineken-owned brand has already seen an uptick in sales in the past year, surpassing $1.4 billion in on-premise sales following a recent launch of a sea salt-spiked lager, according to the Drinks Business.

Luigi Moretti founded Birra Moretti in Udine, Italy, in the Friuli-Venezia Giulia region in 1859 and remained a regional specialty for decades. Heineken picked it up in 1996 and, five years later, began exporting it to international markets. Since the 1940s, Baffo, the stein-drinking man on the label whose table drinkers attempt to set, has been printed on every Birra Moretti bottle, becoming one of the most iconic faces in Italian beer. And with this new trend, Baffo is about to get a lot more popular.

content:
Being a brewer requires a well-honed palate and a keen sense of what is and isn’t good. Brewers exist somewhere on the spectrum of artist to scientist, managing a very precise process while also imbuing their own flourish. Their taste buds and sense of smell are just as important as their fermenters and brew kettles. A brewer is going to know what a good beer is, because they have to know.

But what about those beers that usually wouldn’t be up on a pedestal with the most renowned? The ones that are maligned for being mass-produced, tasting too sweet, piggybacking on an old trend, or (perish the thought) containing pumpkin? There are a slew of beers that the snobbish craft beer nerds would turn their noses up at and refuse to drink. But they may be shocked to learn that brewers often have a favorite among these “guilty pleasure” beers.

So we decided to ask them. We talked to 10 brewers to find out what beers trigger their nostalgia and bring them back again and again. They gushed about unapologetic love for berry ales, cute stubby bottles, and all the brews that live in a soft spot in their hearts.

The best “guilty pleasure” beers, according to brewers:

  • Abita Beer Strawberry Lager
  • Coronitas
  • Young’s Double Chocolate Stout
  • Shipyard Pumpkin Head
  • Busch Light Apple
  • Pabst Blue Ribbon
  • Coors Banquet
  • Miller High Life
  • Industrial Arts Wrench
  • Miller Lite
  • Bud Heavy

“My guilty pleasure beer would have to be Abita Strawberry. It’s hard to say if something is good when nostalgia enters the room. When it comes to flavors, experience can often override that, but this checks all the boxes. Crisp, fruity, and unapologetic. I remember grabbing a sack of crawfish at Fisherman’s Wharf in New Orleans and drinking Abita Strawberry while chowing down on mud bugs overlooking the Mississippi. I still get people to mail it up to me and crush it in my backyard.” —Lara Hargrave, head pub brewer and research and development, Steeplejack Brewing, Portland, Ore.

“My guilty pleasure beer is the little seven-ounce Coronitas. I feel like Andre the Giant when I drink them!” —Richie Tevlin, owner and brewmaster, Space Cadet Brewing Company, Philadelphia

“I still have a soft spot in my heart for Young’s Double Chocolate Stout. It was one of the first stouts I truly loved; richer than a Guinness, but not as sweet as a typical pastry stout. I used to find it in most of my local beer stores, but I haven’t seen it in a while.” —Melissa Walter, co-founder and co-owner, Love City Brewing, Philadelphia

“My guilty pleasure beer is Shipyard Pumpkin Head. The iconic seasonal received a major overhaul in recent years when production was moved to the F.X. Matt brewery. The beer is now lighter in color and leaner in body, leading to a higher drinkability. Fermented with a new yeast strain than it was historically gives it a cleaner finish. The beer is only available three months out of the year, and with its modern upgrades, it will disappear from my fridge faster than ever.” —Michael Fava, beverage director, Novare Res Bier Café, Portland, Maine

“Busch Light Apple is my guilty pleasure. As much as I wanted to hate it when it started trending, I hunt down as much as I reasonably can when I see it drop for the season. And ‘bapple’ is honestly just a cute nickname too.” —Rachael Stillman, brewer, Lost Shoe Brewing and Roasting Company, Marlborough, Mass.

“My guilty pleasure beer is Pabst Blue Ribbon. Reminds me of my college days and is always an easy drinker.” —Tracy Converse, head brewer, Boulder Junction Brewing Company, Boulder Junction, Wis.

content:
Napa and Cabernet Sauvignon are intrinsically linked. The grape brought fame to the region, and in return, the region elevated the grape’s qualities in ways that stood apart from classic winegrowing regions, like Bordeaux. Today, over half of the vineyard acreage is planted to Cabernet Sauvignon, according to Napa Valley Vintners.

There’s no shortage of marquee names in Napa. From cult Cabernets such as Screaming Eagle and Harlan Estate to historically significant producers such as Chateau Montelena and Beaulieu Vineyards to wineries whose style never goes out of fashion, such as Corison, any wine collector worth their cellar can reel off a roster of renowned Napa Cabernet producers. However, these wineries don’t offer a full picture: the valley is filled with smaller, under-the-radar estates producing high-caliber Cabernet. Some aren’t solely focused on Cabernet, either, which means they bring the sensibilities of other varieties into their Cab. And while Napa Cabernet certainly isn’t cheap by any means, there are values to be found. Here are eight lesser-known producers to try if you love Napa Cabernet.

Gallica Wine

Rosemary Cakebread has quietly been influencing Napa palates for over 45 years, first as the former winemaker at Spottswoode and Mumm Napa Valley, before launching her personal label, Gallica, in 2007. At first focused on old-vine Petite Sirah and Cabernet Sauvignon, she expanded to include Grenache and white varieties, such as Chenin Blanc and Albariño. Although 2024 was the last vintage from her St. Helena estate vineyard before replanting commenced, Cabernet from Oakville remains a tentpole in her portfolio. Like her Grenache, the Oakville Cabernet, retailing for around $170, is lithe, elegant, and restrained, with high-tone aromas.

Pestoni Family Estate Winery

Fifth-generation-owned Pestoni sources fruit solely from its three estate vineyards in Howell Mountain, Rutherford, and Quackenbush Mountain in Lake County. As an homage to its founder, Albino Pestoni, who founded the property in 1892, Pestoni continues to cultivate several Italian varieties, such as Sangiovese and Barbera, along with Bordeaux varieties. The Howell Mountain Cabernet, approximately $125, shows lots of bright fruit, finely textured and well-integrated tannins, and a plushness on the palate.

Ashes & Diamonds Winery

Call it the cool kids’ Cabernet. With experiments such as zero-zero winemaking and mentions in Vogue, Ashes & Diamonds has caught the attention of a certain segment of the population that largely eschews Napa. Two primary winemakers oversee different parts of the portfolio: Steve Matthiasson creates blends, and Diana Snowden Seysses focuses on single-vineyard bottlings. All of the wines are restrained yet intensely aromatic. Selling for around $135, the Cabernet No. 6, from the high-elevation Mountain Peak Vineyard, shows intense concentration on the palate.

Benevolent Neglect Wines

Founded in 2013, Benevolent Neglect plays around with a cornucopia of grape varieties. In the lounge-y, vibe-y downtown Napa tasting room, it’s possible to taste Counoise, Riesling, Gamay, and Ribolla Gialla all in one sitting. But Benevolent Neglect, which takes a low-intervention approach to winemaking, also does classic Napa Cabernet. “There’s something to be said for working with traditional grape varieties and seeing how you stack up,” says winemaker Matthew Nagy, who worked with winemakers such as Steve Matthiasson and Thomas Rivers Brown. The Cabernet, which runs about $125, straddles the line between refined and opulent.

Favia Wines

Winemaker Andy Erickson and viticulturist Annie Favia have worked at many of Napa’s premier estates, but Favia, founded in 2003, is the couple’s personal label. It started with a small, five-acre vineyard in Coombsville, and later expanded to a much larger site in Oakville. Both vineyards are farmed organically and biodynamically. The Coombsville property contains light volcanic ash soils and is about 10 degrees cooler than the Oakville site. Both of these elements create a Cabernet, priced at around $250, with minerality and salinity woven throughout the fruit profile.

Pym-Rae

The Tesseron family, who own Bordeaux’s Pontet-Canet, brought their biodynamic farming practices and prowess with Cabernet Sauvignon to Napa over a decade ago, and established Pym-Rae on Mount Veeder. The estate was the former home of the late actor Robin Williams, and the name Pym-Rae comes from the middle names of his children. It’s a plush, elegant wine with lots of tension and minerality, and sells for around $350.

Keplinger Wines

Helen Keplinger’s long and storied career included stints under Napa legend Heidi Barrett, overseas in Spain’s Priorat, and at famed Napa estates such as Bryant Family Vineyard and Grace Estates. Her personal label, Keplinger, in partnership with her husband, DJ Warner, focuses on a global range of wines, from Spanish varieties to Rhône grapes. But, as they split their time between Paso Robles and Napa Valley, Cabernet Sauvignon takes focus. The Oakville Ranch Vineyard Cabernet Sauvignon, which sells for approximately $220, comes from red volcanic soils high on the Vaca mountain range.

No Love Lost Wine Co.

Winemaker Jay Nunez wants to break the standard Napa Valley mold, and his tasting room in downtown Napa shows off the depth and breadth of his creativity. From Mencia to Counoise to Albariño, his low-intervention winemaking highlights all that California has to offer. But, being in Napa, Cabernet Sauvignon still plays a role in the lineup. This Cabernet, however, is a lighter and fresher iteration than many of its neighbors, with bright fruit. At just $75 a bottle, it’s also one of the more affordable Napa Cabernets on the market.

content:
Frozen cocktails have long been a warm-weather staple. But this summer, as we’ve faced the hottest month ever recorded in the U.S. and heat domes dominate the forecast, it’s safe to say Americans are drinking more icy cocktails than ever before.

Frozen Piña Coladas straight from a churning machine and fresh-from-the-blender Daiquiris are often popular picks. But there’s a new, eye-catching method that bartenders are increasingly turning to to make frosty, refreshing cocktails: shaved ice.

At bars and restaurants across the country, bartenders can be found hand-cranking massive machines, spinning hulking blocks of ice across sharp blades to create a fluffy mountain of freshly shaved ice for each drink. New York City’s Tokyo Record Bar added a Japanese-inspired drink with matcha liqueur and shaved ice to the menu to combat this year’s scorching summer. Meanwhile, Kansas’ Wild Child offers up a Midori Sour that resembles a boozy snow cone and East End Hardware in Houston has a slate of icy cocktails on the menu year round.

While more bars are opting into the growing trend this summer, the idea of cooling off with treats made of thinly cut ice is hardly new. From Sno-Balls in New Orleans and Puerto Rican piragua doused in fruit-flavored syrup to Korean bingsu and Filipino halo-halo, shaved ice is popular in dessert from all around the world. But now, cocktail pros are tapping into these longstanding traditions and bringing them over to the bar — one snow cone Martini and kakigori cocktail at a time.

Perfecting the Method

Translating shaved ice from a dessert eaten with a spoon to a version that’s drinkable and served in a glass is no easy task. To get in on this trendy technique, bartenders are painstakingly researching machines from around the world, fine tuning the size of each individual ice chip, and reworking recipes to achieve perfectly textured frozen drinks that can survive the intense dilution that comes from using small pieces of ice.

When NYC’s Bar Kabawa opened its doors in early 2025, it immediately made a splash with its signature Daiquiri, which pours the classic three-ingredient blend of lime juice, sugar, and rum over a towering pile of shaved ice. This puts on quite a show behind the bar, as guests can look on to see bartenders laboriously spin the arm of a large machine, generating a delicate snowfall of soft, frozen shards that falls into each coupe.

At the time, this wasn’t yet a common scene at a cocktail bar. Creative bartender at Bar Kabawa Kathryn “Pepper” Stashek says the first step was finding the right shaved ice machine for the task. At this high-caliber level of bartending, every detail is important and the team at Bar Kabawa went with a hand-crank version that allows them to manually dial in the size of ice chips created by the machine.

At other bars, the tool of choice that has emerged is the traditional machine designed for making kakigori, a Japanese dessert tradition that dates all the way back to the year 1002. In Japan, kakigori is typically made from natural spring water that is frozen and tempered until it becomes crystal clear, just like the cubes and spheres that bars order from specialized producers for drinks. Once the ice is prepared, it is shaved into a bowl and topped with ingredients like condensed milk, mochi, and fresh fruit.

“The drinks are good from the second sip through the very last sip. They tend not to get overdiluted and watery because they don’t reconstitute in the same way as a drink from a blender or frozen machine.”

Some more common types of shaved ice machines create shards that are thick and crunchy, but kakigori machines press the ice so closely against the blade that the pieces are nearly microscopic. When piled high into a glass, the tiny shards get extremely close to each other without combining, creating a fluffy consistency that bartenders love both for its visual appeal and satisfying texture.

In the U.S., most bars employ professional-grade machines that are manufactured in Japan from the company, Swan, which is one of the only options that is certified for food service by the National Sanitation Foundation. To use it, bartenders hoist a cylindrical block of ice, weighing about seven pounds, on top of the machine and turn on a motor that spins the ice over a stationary blade, quickly cutting off paper-thin slices that float into a glass below at a rate of up to five and a half pounds per minute.

Kevin Beary, the beverage director at Gus’ Sip & Dip, says he was drawn to kakigori-style ice over other models and techniques because the consistency is “dead on.” Classic frozen drinks made in a churning frozen machine can end up with separation that makes the cocktail unappealing when it starts to melt. Using shaved ice instead is a great way to avoid that messy situation. “The drinks are good from the second sip through the very last sip,” he says. “They tend not to get overdiluted and watery because they don’t reconstitute in the same way as a drink from a blender or frozen machine.”

Before landing on the Swan machine, which Beary calls the “Cadillac of shaved ice machines,” the team tried a manual, hand-crank model that leaves the ultra-sharp blade more exposed than professional versions. “We were covered in Band-Aids,” Beary says.

The menu at Gus’s Sip and Dip has three drinks served on shaved ice: a classic Margarita, a Hemingway Daiquiri, and a creamy, dessert-like Grasshopper. The Dirty Martini is also effectively garnished with shaved ice as a tiny pile of shavings is dusted on top before serving. Beary shares this was inspired by guests ordering Martinis and asking to “make it skate” by including unstrained ice chips on top. With four drinks showcasing shaved ice, the team goes through 21 large blocks of ice per shift and a large part of prep time involves making the ice in a Clinebell freezer to prepare for the next day’s service.

Shaved ice melts faster than traditional cubes, so bartenders have to account for dilution differently when developing cocktails that will live on a bed of fine, flaky ice. Shaking or stirring with ice can result in a cocktail that’s final volume is anywhere from 15 to 30 percent water — when ice is broken up into smaller pieces, it melts even faster and will add more water than that to the final drink. With that in mind, many bartenders opt to shake or stir the cocktail’s ingredients without ice, instead allowing the drink to naturally dilute as it sits on the bar. “I also liked that the drinks develop over time,” Beary adds.

All About the Look

While the texture is no doubt refreshing, Darryl Chan, the beverage director of NoHo Hospitality Group, says he wanted to introduce shaved ice at The Dutch to add a playful touch to the restaurant’s dedicated Martini Bar offerings. The menu launched earlier this summer, featuring a drink called the Dirty Snow Cone, a briny vodka Martini with a touch of Chartreuse Élixir Végétal served in a cone of shaved ice. “It’s a fun presentation. There’s an art to it,” says Chan. “In a city full of serious Martini drinkers, I wanted to take the Martini and not make it so precious.”

Chan originally developed the cocktail for Tales of the Cocktail, an annual event when the industry descends upon New Orleans amid its swampiest season. When spiked snow cones were handed over the bar, the sight stopped parched and tipsy bartenders in their tracks at the event — and Chan was certain it would have the same appeal during a toasty NYC summer.

From the avalanche of shaved ice coming off the machine to the ice collapsing on itself in the glass, Chan says the drink provides a show from start to finish. In an era where unconventional garnishes are commonplace and people head to the bar in search of both showmanship and expert-crafted drinks, guests have quickly latched on. “People come in wanting to order it or they see tables getting four of them and end up ordering,” he says. “It definitely turns heads.”

For others, like Stashek at Bar Kabawa, the showmanship that comes with serving shaved ice was simply a “fun side effect” of making an excellent drink that nods to the way Daiquiris were first served in Havana.

”People ooh and aah, and that’s awesome, but that certainly was not the main focus when we were developing it,” she says. “We really lucked out. Videos and social media stuff are an important part of being in the food and beverage scene right now, but it really happened organically for us.”

content:
In some parts of the United States, it still feels like 1920. When the federal government repealed Prohibition in 1933, it left the decision on how to legislate the production and sale of wine, beer, and spirits to the individual states. State governments then handed alcohol regulation to towns, counties, and other municipalities, and laws on drinking diversified to a fine-tooth comb level across the country. A “dry” county, meaning it prohibits the sale of alcoholic beverages, could neighbor a fully “wet” county, one that permits the sale of alcoholic beverages.

Ninety-three years later, some counties across the U.S. are still dry, and the reasons behind the abstinences range from historic to religious.

Below, we mapped out the 47 counties in the U.S. that still prohibit the sale of alcohol. What is most evident at first glance is the concentration of teetotalling neighborhoods in the South, along what’s otherwise known as the “Bible Belt,” dubbed so because of the region’s high density of practicing Christians. In Arkansas, the state with the most dry counties at 29, sects like Methodists, Baptists, and Evangelicals — the latter makes up roughly 50 percent of Arkansas’ population — have promoted abstaining from alcohol since the 1800s. In 1831, local churches in the state aligned to form the Little Rock Temperance Society.

Temperance was also historically associated with the women’s rights movement of the mid-19th century, particularly in Kentucky, where there are six dry counties. Advocates of a prohibition warned of how alcohol worsened some men’s maltreatment of women at home. One Kentucky native, Carrie Nation, famously wielded a hatchet around towns, hacking at the walls and doors at saloons and clubs.

Some counties returned to teetotalism after Prohibition’s repeal. In Arkansas’ Craighead and Crawford counties, current accounts attribute the alcohol ban to municipal votes that occurred in 1944 when many American men were overseas fighting in the Second World War, and at-combat soldiers could not cast their ballots. Since then, petitions to turn wet have yet to amass enough voters. Just getting the question to permit alcohol on ballots in certain counties requires a much larger percentage of voters than most other issues.

Other reasons that some counties across the U.S. remain dry include low population and lobbying from successful liquor stores in nearby wet counties who fear losing business, among others.

The map below omits the in-between examples, referred to as “moist” counties. While these counties are de jure dry, they leave the decision up to each local government, so regulations vary from town to town. The map does include dry counties that allow special permits to certain on-premise accounts, such as country clubs, restaurants, and other businesses.

News to know:

The analytics and advisory firm included a question on nonalcoholic beverage consumption for the first time in its annual survey and found only 17 percent of U.S. citizens substituted a zero-proof wine, beer, or spirit for an alcoholic drink at least once in the past year.
  • Diageo cuts roughly 2,000 jobs in restructuring plan: The global spirits giant slimmed its workforce by six percent year-over-year through the end of June, according to its annual report. The results come after Diageo chief executive officer Dave Lewis denied to disclose the number of roles the overhaul would affect when announcing a $1 billion savings plan involving reducing prices and cutting jobs. According to Reuters, the company is set to complete its workforce reduction by Sept. 1, meaning it’s possible the number of impacted jobs can increase.
  • Boston Beer Company workers plan to unionize: Employees at the Samuel Adams Boston Brewery in Jamaica Plain, Mass. — Boston Beer Co.’s first and flagship brewery — filed an intent to unionize to the parent company last Thursday. Workers included in the possible union include bartenders, cooks, beer ambassadors, and key holders, according to the United Food and Commercial Workers Union Local 328, who first reported on the filing. The organization would be the second Samuel Adams location with a union.
  • Sazerac to ink a deal with Welsh vodka brand: The Louisville, Ky.-based spirits company agreed to acquire Au Vodka, a buzzy brand in the U.K., for a reported £500 million ($681 million). Au Vodka will join Sazerac’s portfolio well-stocked in brands geared toward Gen Z drinkers like BuzzBallz and sipMARGS.

  • Pernod Ricard ships Single Pot Still Jameson to U.S. shores: Jameson, the leading Irish whiskey brand by volume, is debuting its Distiller’s Batch bottling in American markets. Distiller’s Batch is part of the brand’s premium Reserve Series and will be available nationwide in September.

content:
Made with a commitment to both honoring tradition and embracing innovation, G4 Tequila is the latest brand to win over the bar industry amid the artisanal tequila renaissance.

With deep family roots in the industry, Felipe Camarena founded the distillery that houses G4’s production in 2007 before its official opening in 2011. The brand didn’t reach shelves in the United States until 2014, but in the past decade, it’s become one of the foremost choices among bar pros and tequila enthusiasts.

G4 aims to honor the history and tradition of tequila while ushering the spirit into the new age, converging old-school ingredients and techniques with new-school technology. From the meaning behind the name to the brand’s meticulous production methods, here are seven things to know about G4 Tequila.

  1. The name refers to Camarena’s family lineage.

    Felipe Camarena is the great-grandson of Don Pedro Camarena, a legendary tequilero often credited with being among the first to bring Blue Weber agave to the highlands in the 19th century. The family has continued in the business over the years, making Felipe Camarena the fourth generation to work in the tequila industry, inspiring the name “G4.”

    Don Pedro built the Camarena family’s first distillery in Los Altos, before it crumbled upon the onset of the Mexican Revolution in 1910. Don Pedro’s son, also named Felipe, opened the family’s second distillery, La Alteña, which is now home to brands like Tapatio and Tequila Ocho. Felipe used to work at La Alteña, but left in 2007 to construct his own distillery, El Pandillo.

  2. You’ll be drinking rainwater — sort of.

    G4 — and all brands produced at El Pandillo, for that matter — sources both spring water and rainwater to make its tequila. The brand’s blanco expression uses a half-and-half split between the two water types, which its website says helps create “an authentic, beyond-organic experience.” Other accounts agree and call it the “secret” to its greatness, saying the rainwater imparts a “wet-stone minerality” to the spirit. El Pandillo retrieves rainwater through a capturing system built on the distillery’s roof, funneling it into a 200,000-liter underground tank.

  3. The master distiller invented a custom agave-crushing machine.

    Camarena studied engineering and used his gadget-building side to invent an agave crusher. Named Felipestein as a nod to “Frankenstein,” the machine is 19,000-pounds, built entirely from recycled parts of a railroad car, steamroller, and other industrial materials. Felipestein, studded with spikes, rolls along rail tracks, crushing cooked agave along the way. Camarena has found that this unique method presses the plant’s juices without tearing its fibers.

  4. G4 uses an ancestral yeast strain.

    Camarena dials into his family’s tequila-making legacy even further by using a strain of agave yeast preserved from his grandfather, Don Felipe, who opened La Alteña in 1937. Don Felipe passed down the yeast for generations, helping preserve the Camarena family’s identity in its tequilas.

  5. The brand has a proprietary tequila certification course.

    G4 collaborated with the International Tequila Academy to form its own training curriculum for tequila-interested consumers. Retailers, bartenders, or aficionados who simply want to learn more about the brand, its history, and process, can follow the online course. The curriculum covers tequila production, G4’s products, and the ins and outs of the spirits market.

  6. G4’s site features the one surviving piece of the Camarena family’s original distillery.

    Little remains of Don Pedro Camarena’s original distillery that burned down during the Mexican Revolution. One of its remnants is the volcanic stone tahona that was used at the Los Altos location — it was the tool the family used to make its first-ever batch of tequila. The tahona is now on display at El Pandillo.

  7. The brand is expanding — and adding new products.

    Given its smashing popularity in recent years, G4 is scaling upward, and along with this growth came a new storage facility that neighbors El Pandillo. There, G4 is experimenting with different aging techniques and barrel types. For example, it recently announced that it will mature some of its tequila in lightly used Jack Daniel’s casks. It will also experiment with other vessels, including ex-Cognac, sherry, and wine barrels.

title: Tilray Keeps Closing Craft Breweries Because Its Strategy Never Made Sense in the First Place
summary:
For years, the comedian Ron White has done a joke about the time he almost got in a plane crash. It’s an all-timer that unravels over the course of a few minutes, and you really owe it to yourself to watch the whole thing. I hate to spoil the punch line, but the joke is about 30 years old, so with respect to Mr. White, here goes: The guy sitting next to me is losing his mind. Apparently, he had a lot to live for.

The article Tilray Keeps Closing Craft Breweries Because Its Strategy Never Made Sense in the First Place appeared first on VinePair.
content:
For years, the comedian Ron White has done a joke about the time he almost got in a plane crash. It’s an all-timer that unravels over the course of a few minutes, and you really owe it to yourself to watch the whole thing. I hate to spoil the punch line, but the joke is about 30 years old, so with respect to Mr. White, here goes:

The guy sitting next to me is losing his mind. Apparently, he had a lot to live for.

He goes, “Hey man … huh-huh-huh … hey man … huh-huh-huh … If one of these engines fails, how far will the other one take us?”

[I said] “All the way to the scene of the crash … which is pretty handy, because that’s where we’re headed. I bet we beat the paramedics there by a half hour.”

Classic stuff. And unfortunately clarifying stuff for the situation at Tilray Brands, whose overstuffed portfolio of craft breweries is well on its way to where it was always headed.

Last week, news broke that the Canadian vice conglomerate planned to close Terrapin Beer Company’s 100,000-square-foot production facility in Athens, Ga. The University of Georgia’s independent student-run paper, The Red & Black, first clocked the shutdown notice, which was buried in Tilray’s most recent 10-K filing. The document also flagged previous consolidations and closures at Hop Valley, Revolver, and Redhook, as well as Atwater, which wasn’t “closed” so much as “hastily sold back to its owners less than two years after it was acquired.” But forget the semantics, let’s talk strategy, because it’s pretty complicated. Just kidding: we’re cutting costs, kids!

Shortly after cobbling together its island of misfit breweries from the wreckage of macrobrewers’ salad-days craft beer ambitions, Tilray embarked upon Project 420, which is not the Heritage Foundation’s plan to make smoking weed a capital offense but rather a goofily named corporate savings strategy. (SweetWater Brewing, its first major acquisition in the segment in 2020, does a 420 Extra Pale Ale and a 420 Fest, too. You get it.) Midway through 2025, the firm’s garrulous chief executive, Irwin Simon, told investors that he was targeting some $33 million in cuts, which doesn’t sound like a lot until you remember it’s almost half of what he paid for an eight-brand gaggle of Anheuser-Busch InBev also-rans just a couple years prior. By the end of February 2026, the company’s filing reads, “we considered the Project 420 plan to be completed due to reaching the cost savings target that we had set out to achieve even though there are still ongoing initiatives relating to additional cost savings, SKU rationalization and distributor rationalization.” Whether Terrapin’s closure is technically part of Project 420, or whatever its new-and-reduced successor program is called within the halls of Tilray headquarters is irrelevant for our purposes. It’s another cut.

Pour one out for Terrapin’s poor workers and fans, who have been through the wringer over the past decade as the company went from a Southeastern craft-brewing darling to an odious sellout to big bad Molson Coors, to a cast-off has-been when Simon and company came calling in the summer of 2024. But where there’s sorrow, there should be little surprise. Simon’s “regional jewel” thesis for batting cleanup on the craft-brewing industry’s second boom, which he articulated to Hop Take in December 2024, never made sense without major cuts, even at the bargain-basement purchase prices he was able to command from the bigs as they bolted for flavored malt beverages and spirits-based canned cocktails. This wasn’t something Tilray was openly talking about at that point, mind you, but it was evident even then. As I wrote:

Whatever Tilray does to burnish its “regional jewels” in bars, restaurants, and sports venues will ultimately have to be judged by whether it successfully repositions those brands for distributed sales — and whether it can actually drive down its costs like Simon claims.

The latter is absurd on face: Tilray lacks the buying power of ABI or MC (or Constellation, Heineken, Pabst… ), and its operations are scattered across many small locations rather than a few big ones. Simon concedes that point to Hop Take, but insists that Tilray can unlock savings anyway by integrating these brands into a national operation in a way their former corporate masters failed to.

More than a year and a half later, whatever sweet synergies Tilray has been able to capture with its mid-major scale have paled in comparison to those savings it has been able to extract from the business in the form of layoffs, plant closures, and portfolio weed-outs. This hasn’t come cheaply, mind you. As my VinePair colleague Stephen Bradley noted, “Tilray disclosed it spent $6.8 million in Project 420 restructuring costs in fiscal year 2026, which ended May 31.” That’s on top of the $8.5 million it already spent on the slash-a-rama in 2025, per the 10-K.

This spend-and-shed pattern has become a bit of a calling card for Tilray, which earlier this year acquired BrewDog at the rock-bottom price of~ $54 million and announced a deal to brew Carlsberg stateside shortly thereafter. Even as it was culling its craft-brewing herd, in other words, it was adding to it. The results have been mixed. The company’s beverage business grew net revenue by six percent year-over-year for its 2026 fiscal year, which ran through May; its gross profit was down two percent for the same period. But that’s including the big ol’ boost that BrewDog delivered to its stat-sheet. (Here too, another calling card of Simon and company: before the dust can really settle on the previous fiscal year’s acquisitions, he’s already bought something else, juicing the topline numbers while making it harder to benchmark the firm against its actual performance in the marketplace.) The drinks business remains “one of Tilray’s most important growth engines,” Simon told investors on an earnings call late last month, and is “still in the early stages of unlocking the full potential of this business.”

That may sound good to Wall Street. (Or not: Tilray’s troubled stock declined a smidge following the July 28 call, before rallying more recently.) But it rings ominous when you consider how the company has made it this far on its craft-brewing side-quest. While it waits and hopes for federal legalization of recreational cannabis, it has to make its mismatched semi-national network of breweries produce meaningful revenue. It can only book the savings from closing each brewery once. At some point, Tilray must squeeze actual, consistent profit out of these brands. I thought — and still do — that the company had lined up plenty of runway by buying into the segment at such firesale prices. It has lined up more still with all its cuts. But whether anybody wants what’s left on the other side of the butcher counter remains to be seen. The sales data suggest, ah, maybe not. Year-to-date through July 12, Tilray’s portfolio is down 13.7 percent in dollars and 14.8 percent by volume in multi-outlet grocery, mass retail, and convenience stores tracked by the market research firm Circana. Those declines dramatically overshadow the overall beer category and the craft-brewing segment

This is the rub. “With robust brewing operations across the country, this transition allows us to continue serving customers efficiently while leveraging the scale and capabilities of our broader brewery footprint,” chief corporate affairs officer Berrin Noorata told Brewbound in a statement. The optimization jargon tracks with the basics of the brewing business: it is a scale business. But while sending Terrapin’s brewhouse to the Hopsecutioner may carve out costs, it also hollows out the brand itself. Even with healthy brands — which Tilray’s, by and large, are not — it’s hard to tell muscle from fat. But in a down market this competitive, shuttering a hometown brewery promises some real rough turbulence.

This was always where Tilray was headed. Where it goes next remains to be seen.

🤯 Hop-ocalypse Now

Summer 2026 has not been kind to Bud Light, what with its bleak bloodsport-’n-bigotry sponsorship of the Trump administration’s Ultimate Fighting Championship circus on the White House lawn, and of course the brand’s ongoing declines as both the American drinking public and parent company Anheuser-Busch InBev shift their focus to stuff like Michelob Ultra, Cutwater, and BeatBox. Complicating matters further, one of the celebrities the brand hired to chud up its image in the wake of 2023’s right-wing transphobia tantrum, comedian Shane Gillis, last week spoke out against Truth Social’s transparently corrupt scheme to sell early access to Trump’s posts on the platform, calling it “literally insider trading.” And on an episode of “The Joe Rogan Experience,” no less! Awkward stuff for a brand that has been desperately cozying up to the MAGA-verse for the past three years.

📈 Ups…

TailGate Brewery is telling a Tennessee success story, up 40 percent in distribution year-over-year through the first half of 2026… Garage Beer released an apple-flavored version, because who doesn’t want free money?… Hi-Wire Brewing is taking over production and sales for Appalachian Mountain Brewery as craft consolidation continues…

📉 …and downs

Boston Beer Company’s chief financial officer is headed for the exit… Ardagh Metal Packaging is on the auction block…

Drinking beers and household chores never had much in common, but now, you can “set the table” while knocking back a half-goblet of lager. In the latest beer challenge to sweep the internet, people are guzzling Birra Moretti in an attempt to align the liquid’s surface with the mustachioed man on the beer’s label. The goal: make it look like his arm is resting on a table of beer.

This trend offers a new spin on Guinness’ megawatt “splitting the G” phenomenon, roughly two years after the now-iconic gulping-guessing game swarmed pubs and social media platforms. The challenge likely emerged as a bar game, but it appears to have become a worldwide fad after popular TikTok and Instagram accounts posted carousels and videos of successful table-sets and garnered tens of thousands of views and likes.

@the.white.horse.southill Drink responsibly kings and queens ✌🏻 #fyp #moretti #beer #hospitality #pub ♬ original sound – Ibiza Records

Just as some devotees met “splitting the G” with disdain, certain beer purists are gawking at the challenge. “Can’t you just drink your beer like a normal person?,” one Instagram user commented on LADBible’s post, the first to broadcast the challenge.

While you can find a solid pint of Guinness in a branded glass to partake in “splitting the G” at just about any pub, hunting down Birra Moretti in the signature goblet isn’t as easy. But with “setting the table” on the rise, the brand is only poised to become more popular.

The Heineken-owned brand has already seen an uptick in sales in the past year, surpassing $1.4 billion in on-premise sales following a recent launch of a sea salt-spiked lager, according to the Drinks Business.

Luigi Moretti founded Birra Moretti in Udine, Italy, in the Friuli-Venezia Giulia region in 1859 and remained a regional specialty for decades. Heineken picked it up in 1996 and, five years later, began exporting it to international markets. Since the 1940s, Baffo, the stein-drinking man on the label whose table drinkers attempt to set, has been printed on every Birra Moretti bottle, becoming one of the most iconic faces in Italian beer. And with this new trend, Baffo is about to get a lot more popular.

content:
Being a brewer requires a well-honed palate and a keen sense of what is and isn’t good. Brewers exist somewhere on the spectrum of artist to scientist, managing a very precise process while also imbuing their own flourish. Their taste buds and sense of smell are just as important as their fermenters and brew kettles. A brewer is going to know what a good beer is, because they have to know.

But what about those beers that usually wouldn’t be up on a pedestal with the most renowned? The ones that are maligned for being mass-produced, tasting too sweet, piggybacking on an old trend, or (perish the thought) containing pumpkin? There are a slew of beers that the snobbish craft beer nerds would turn their noses up at and refuse to drink. But they may be shocked to learn that brewers often have a favorite among these “guilty pleasure” beers.

So we decided to ask them. We talked to 10 brewers to find out what beers trigger their nostalgia and bring them back again and again. They gushed about unapologetic love for berry ales, cute stubby bottles, and all the brews that live in a soft spot in their hearts.

The best “guilty pleasure” beers, according to brewers:

  • Abita Beer Strawberry Lager
  • Coronitas
  • Young’s Double Chocolate Stout
  • Shipyard Pumpkin Head
  • Busch Light Apple
  • Pabst Blue Ribbon
  • Coors Banquet
  • Miller High Life
  • Industrial Arts Wrench
  • Miller Lite
  • Bud Heavy

“My guilty pleasure beer would have to be Abita Strawberry. It’s hard to say if something is good when nostalgia enters the room. When it comes to flavors, experience can often override that, but this checks all the boxes. Crisp, fruity, and unapologetic. I remember grabbing a sack of crawfish at Fisherman’s Wharf in New Orleans and drinking Abita Strawberry while chowing down on mud bugs overlooking the Mississippi. I still get people to mail it up to me and crush it in my backyard.” —Lara Hargrave, head pub brewer and research and development, Steeplejack Brewing, Portland, Ore.

“My guilty pleasure beer is the little seven-ounce Coronitas. I feel like Andre the Giant when I drink them!” —Richie Tevlin, owner and brewmaster, Space Cadet Brewing Company, Philadelphia

“I still have a soft spot in my heart for Young’s Double Chocolate Stout. It was one of the first stouts I truly loved; richer than a Guinness, but not as sweet as a typical pastry stout. I used to find it in most of my local beer stores, but I haven’t seen it in a while.” —Melissa Walter, co-founder and co-owner, Love City Brewing, Philadelphia

“My guilty pleasure beer is Shipyard Pumpkin Head. The iconic seasonal received a major overhaul in recent years when production was moved to the F.X. Matt brewery. The beer is now lighter in color and leaner in body, leading to a higher drinkability. Fermented with a new yeast strain than it was historically gives it a cleaner finish. The beer is only available three months out of the year, and with its modern upgrades, it will disappear from my fridge faster than ever.” —Michael Fava, beverage director, Novare Res Bier Café, Portland, Maine

“Busch Light Apple is my guilty pleasure. As much as I wanted to hate it when it started trending, I hunt down as much as I reasonably can when I see it drop for the season. And ‘bapple’ is honestly just a cute nickname too.” —Rachael Stillman, brewer, Lost Shoe Brewing and Roasting Company, Marlborough, Mass.

“My guilty pleasure beer is Pabst Blue Ribbon. Reminds me of my college days and is always an easy drinker.” —Tracy Converse, head brewer, Boulder Junction Brewing Company, Boulder Junction, Wis.

“My guilty pleasure beer was Coors Banquet, specifically the stubby bottles. But then I moved to Wisconsin and had to switch to the Champagne of Beers, Miller High Life. It’s crisp, refreshing, and reliable. And my other guilty pleasure is the Real Housewives franchise. The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City came to Milwaukee and drank High Life, so if it’s good enough for Real Housewives, it’s good enough for this small brewer.” —Erica DeAnda, brewmaster, Tumbled Rock Brewery and Kitchen, Baraboo, Wis.

“My guilty pleasure beer has to be a hazy IPA since we all (brewers) pretend to hate them. Wrench by Industrial Arts is always going to take it. Impressively consistent, always tasty, refreshing, always sticky! The NA version is also a secret obsession of mine right now.” —Andreina Uribe, cellarperson, Grimm Artisanal Ales, Brooklyn

“Miller Lite. It was always around growing up at friends’ parent’s houses, so there’s a nostalgia to it for me. Even then, I remember thinking it had a little more flavor than the other light beers around. It still tastes like summer weekends, cookouts, and garage beers with the homies.” —Jay Neveu, general manager, Phantom Farms Brewing, Cumberland, R.I.

“I would say Bud Heavy! When I was born, my family lived in a trailer, and there’s just something about a Bud Heavy that takes me back to those early days.” —Theo Castillo, founder and brewer, No Seasons, Miami

content:
Napa and Cabernet Sauvignon are intrinsically linked. The grape brought fame to the region, and in return, the region elevated the grape’s qualities in ways that stood apart from classic winegrowing regions, like Bordeaux. Today, over half of the vineyard acreage is planted to Cabernet Sauvignon, according to Napa Valley Vintners.

There’s no shortage of marquee names in Napa. From cult Cabernets such as Screaming Eagle and Harlan Estate to historically significant producers such as Chateau Montelena and Beaulieu Vineyards to wineries whose style never goes out of fashion, such as Corison, any wine collector worth their cellar can reel off a roster of renowned Napa Cabernet producers. However, these wineries don’t offer a full picture: the valley is filled with smaller, under-the-radar estates producing high-caliber Cabernet. Some aren’t solely focused on Cabernet, either, which means they bring the sensibilities of other varieties into their Cab. And while Napa Cabernet certainly isn’t cheap by any means, there are values to be found. Here are eight lesser-known producers to try if you love Napa Cabernet.

Gallica Wine

Rosemary Cakebread has quietly been influencing Napa palates for over 45 years, first as the former winemaker at Spottswoode and Mumm Napa Valley, before launching her personal label, Gallica, in 2007. At first focused on old-vine Petite Sirah and Cabernet Sauvignon, she expanded to include Grenache and white varieties, such as Chenin Blanc and Albariño. Although 2024 was the last vintage from her St. Helena estate vineyard before replanting commenced, Cabernet from Oakville remains a tentpole in her portfolio. Like her Grenache, the Oakville Cabernet, retailing for around $170, is lithe, elegant, and restrained, with high-tone aromas.

Pestoni Family Estate Winery

Fifth-generation-owned Pestoni sources fruit solely from its three estate vineyards in Howell Mountain, Rutherford, and Quackenbush Mountain in Lake County. As an homage to its founder, Albino Pestoni, who founded the property in 1892, Pestoni continues to cultivate several Italian varieties, such as Sangiovese and Barbera, along with Bordeaux varieties. The Howell Mountain Cabernet, approximately $125, shows lots of bright fruit, finely textured and well-integrated tannins, and a plushness on the palate.

Ashes & Diamonds Winery

Call it the cool kids’ Cabernet. With experiments such as zero-zero winemaking and mentions in Vogue, Ashes & Diamonds has caught the attention of a certain segment of the population that largely eschews Napa. Two primary winemakers oversee different parts of the portfolio: Steve Matthiasson creates blends, and Diana Snowden Seysses focuses on single-vineyard bottlings. All of the wines are restrained yet intensely aromatic. Selling for around $135, the Cabernet No. 6, from the high-elevation Mountain Peak Vineyard, shows intense concentration on the palate.

Benevolent Neglect Wines

Founded in 2013, Benevolent Neglect plays around with a cornucopia of grape varieties. In the lounge-y, vibe-y downtown Napa tasting room, it’s possible to taste Counoise, Riesling, Gamay, and Ribolla Gialla all in one sitting. But Benevolent Neglect, which takes a low-intervention approach to winemaking, also does classic Napa Cabernet. “There’s something to be said for working with traditional grape varieties and seeing how you stack up,” says winemaker Matthew Nagy, who worked with winemakers such as Steve Matthiasson and Thomas Rivers Brown. The Cabernet, which runs about $125, straddles the line between refined and opulent.

Favia Wines

Winemaker Andy Erickson and viticulturist Annie Favia have worked at many of Napa’s premier estates, but Favia, founded in 2003, is the couple’s personal label. It started with a small, five-acre vineyard in Coombsville, and later expanded to a much larger site in Oakville. Both vineyards are farmed organically and biodynamically. The Coombsville property contains light volcanic ash soils and is about 10 degrees cooler than the Oakville site. Both of these elements create a Cabernet, priced at around $250, with minerality and salinity woven throughout the fruit profile.

Pym-Rae

The Tesseron family, who own Bordeaux’s Pontet-Canet, brought their biodynamic farming practices and prowess with Cabernet Sauvignon to Napa over a decade ago, and established Pym-Rae on Mount Veeder. The estate was the former home of the late actor Robin Williams, and the name Pym-Rae comes from the middle names of his children. It’s a plush, elegant wine with lots of tension and minerality, and sells for around $350.

Keplinger Wines

Helen Keplinger’s long and storied career included stints under Napa legend Heidi Barrett, overseas in Spain’s Priorat, and at famed Napa estates such as Bryant Family Vineyard and Grace Estates. Her personal label, Keplinger, in partnership with her husband, DJ Warner, focuses on a global range of wines, from Spanish varieties to Rhône grapes. But, as they split their time between Paso Robles and Napa Valley, Cabernet Sauvignon takes focus. The Oakville Ranch Vineyard Cabernet Sauvignon, which sells for approximately $220, comes from red volcanic soils high on the Vaca mountain range.

No Love Lost Wine Co.

Winemaker Jay Nunez wants to break the standard Napa Valley mold, and his tasting room in downtown Napa shows off the depth and breadth of his creativity. From Mencia to Counoise to Albariño, his low-intervention winemaking highlights all that California has to offer. But, being in Napa, Cabernet Sauvignon still plays a role in the lineup. This Cabernet, however, is a lighter and fresher iteration than many of its neighbors, with bright fruit. At just $75 a bottle, it’s also one of the more affordable Napa Cabernets on the market.

Founded by Allen Katz, an entrepreneur obsessed with cocktails and the bars creating them, the distillery sought out to specifically target New York-based bartenders. Katz also turned New York Distilling into a destination for the liquid-curious, opening a hands-on experience in Williamsburg for both aficionados and novices. Since its founding, the brand has become a mainstay behind bars across New York, but Katz always believed it could become something bigger — an ambition ultimately led him to sell the company.

On this episode of “The Buildout,” Allen joins Adam to discuss founding one of New York State’s first distilleries after Prohibition, building the brand, and preparing it to go global.
